title: Conformal Optimistic Prediction
one_liner: When the world changes unfairly, make prediction bands tighter by learning from past mistakes instead of always playing it safe.
lead: Conformal prediction is a way to wrap a model's answer in a band of uncertainty that is guaranteed to include the true answer at least a certain fraction of the time. The problem: when data patterns shift around (like a thermometer that moves, then suddenly starts drifting), today's methods get scared and make those bands wider and wider, missing easy chances to tighten them when the pattern becomes predictable again. COP learns from the data's own rhythm and adjusts the bands dynamically.

problem.h2: The world shifts, but safety can be overdone
paras: Imagine a model that predicts next week's temperature. It learns from years of data and makes predictions. But real weather patterns shift: a 10-year climate trend, a seasonal flip, even weird anomalies. A smart model detects some shifts but not all, and its predictions drift further from the truth.
A prediction band is a range (like 'between 65 and 75 degrees') that the model promises will contain the true answer some fraction of the time—say, 90 percent. That promise is a legal obligation.

A naive method: measure how wrong the model was on old examples. Take the worst-case mistakes and add that safety margin to every new prediction. Problem: if the world has shifted smoothly and become slightly more predictable (because a seasonal pattern kicked in), this method still adds the maximum safety margin, wasting the opportunity to give a narrow, useful band. It sees only drift, not rhythm. It says 'I cannot trust change, so I will stay maximally cautious forever.'

callout.html: Learn how often the model's errors come back to haunt it, and use that rhythm to tighten the bands when the pattern is predictable—while keeping the guarantee if the pattern breaks.

panels.title: 1. Model learns from the past
panels.caption: Trained on weather data, the model learns to predict tomorrow's temperature.

panels.title: 2. Old method: worst case forever
panels.caption: Takes the biggest error ever and adds it to every band. Safe, but wasteful.

panels.title: 3. COP learns the error pattern
panels.caption: Watches how errors clump over time. Recent errors hint at what to expect next.

panels.title: 4. The estimated curve
panels.caption: Builds a picture of where error scores are now, not where they were years ago.

panels.title: 5. Tighter bands emerge
panels.caption: Narrows the prediction band when the pattern is stable, widens when chaos returns.

steps.text: Collect how wrong the model was on the last, say, 100 examples.
From those 100 errors, estimate where the next error is likely to fall.
Pick a threshold (a value on that curve) that guarantees the band will be right 90 percent of the time.
Instead of blindly following online learning rules, slide the threshold slightly based on recent errors, leveraging the curve's shape.
Apply the threshold to the new prediction, observe the outcome, and update the curve.

paras: The core change is in how the threshold for the prediction band is updated each round. Old methods take a step in a fixed direction (usually down when errors are small, up when they are large). COP adds a nudge based on an estimated picture of where error scores are likely to land. This makes the step smarter because the nudge corrects for the real shape of the error pattern, so the threshold lands closer to the optimal value in fewer rounds, saving computational work and reaching stable band widths faster.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: error pattern from past observations
hidden.name: Estimated CDF of error scores
paras: COP builds a picture of past errors by asking: 'what fraction of my recent mistakes fell below each size level?' This picture, called a cumulative distribution function (or CDF, the running tally of how often errors landed in each size bucket), is built from observed data without any assumptions about normal or special shape.

The paper uses this picture to refine the update step. Instead of always moving the threshold by the same amount, it asks: 'Given the errors I have seen so far, where should the threshold move to keep coverage stable while making the band tighter?' This is the hidden mechanism—a learned model of where errors cluster that guides the algorithm.

heat.caption: Darker means COP learns this error score is more common. Boxes mark where the algorithm pushes hardest.

reads.html: The algorithm remembers how often past errors fell into each size bucket. When a new prediction arrives, COP guesses 'based on that memory, what error am I likely to see?' and tightens the band accordingly.

COP builds the CDF of non-conformity scores from recent data and uses it in a refinement step based on linear approximation of the expected quantile loss. The CDF is not inverted; instead, it enters directly into the update computation, making the algorithm both efficient and theoretically grounded.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the smart update chain
paras: COP balances two competing goals: online learning (adapting to any distribution shift) and distribution information (narrowing bands when patterns repeat).

Imagine standing at a threshold value (say, 42). Each round, you receive a new error score. Online learning would say: 'If the error exceeded my threshold, slide the threshold up a bit; if it stayed below, slide down.' This is safe but slow—it takes many rounds to find a good resting place when the world stabilizes.

COP does something smarter. It computes where the threshold 'should' be according to the recent distribution of errors, using a linear approximation of the quantile loss function (which measures how wrong the threshold is). Then it slides in that direction, weighted by confidence in the distribution estimate. If the estimate is noisy or the world is chaotic, the step is small; if the pattern is clear and stable, the step is larger. This lets COP tighten bands quickly when safe to do so, yet back off if chaos returns.

stages.s: Error score and old threshold value
Compute expected quantile loss at current and candidate thresholds
Estimate CDF of recent scores; extract the implied optimal direction
Take a step along that direction, scaled by learning rate
New threshold that balances coverage and tightness

math.words: Expected quantile loss, then refined with distribution estimate
math.equation: ell_{1-alpha}(q) = (1{q > 0} - alpha) * q;  q_{t+1} = q_t - eta * [predicted gradient at q_t using estimated CDF]
symbols: the threshold (the boundary of the prediction band) at timestep t
the error rate we are willing to tolerate (e.g. 0.1 means 90 percent coverage target)
the non-conformity score (how far the model's prediction was from the truth) at timestep t
the quantile loss function, which is zero if we guessed right and grows if the threshold is wrong
the step size (how boldly we move the threshold)
the estimated cumulative distribution of past scores—what fraction of errors fall below each value

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Setup: target coverage alpha=0.1 (90%), current threshold q=50, recent errors average around 45.
Step 1: Quantile loss at q=50 with error s=45: loss = (1{50>0} - 0.1) * 50 = 0.9 * 50 = 45.
Step 2: Estimated CDF says 80% of recent errors were <= 45, so the implied optimal threshold is around 45.
Step 3: Gradient from CDF shape suggests moving down by about 3 units. With step size eta=0.2, we move: 50 - 0.2 * 3 = 49.4.
Step 4: On the next example with error 44, the band is slightly tighter; if error jumps to 60, the band widens again.

math.note: The estimated CDF replaces a fixed worst-case margin with a learned curve that adapts to the actual error distribution.

bars.h2: Coverage and band width over time

charts.title: Naive worst-case method
charts.note: Safe but rigid. Adds the largest historical error to every band, never tightens even when patterns stabilize.

charts.title: COP with distribution learning
charts.note: Maintains coverage while cutting band width in half when patterns are clear, and recovers quickly when the world destabilizes.

items.html: In the first few rounds, the estimated CDF is noisy because there are only a handful of past errors to build it from. COP's step size shrinks, so it does not over-correct, but the bands start wide and tighten gradually.

If the world shifts radically (like a sensor breaks or a new data source arrives), the estimated CDF from recent errors no longer matches what is coming. COP will over-tighten for a round or two, risking coverage violation, until new error samples retrain the CDF.
Too large an eta, and COP chases every random fluctuation; too small, and it lags behind real shifts. The paper analyzes how to set eta but the practitioner must still choose or tune it per problem.

If eta is set appropriately for the problem (via cross-validation or held-out regret analysis), COP maintains coverage guarantees while exploiting predictable patterns, cutting band width in half on stable data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate a synthetic time series where the model's errors follow a pattern: e.g., errors come from a normal distribution with slowly drifting mean, then suddenly jump to heavy-tailed at timestep 1000. Split into three regimes: stable, drift, chaos. For each regime, measure coverage (did the band contain the true value?) and band width. Compare COP against a fixed worst-case method and against online learning without distribution estimates. COP should show: narrow bands during stable and drift phases because it learns where errors cluster and moves the threshold directly toward the learned optimum, not one blind step at a time; coverage holds in all three regimes because it never forgets the safety principle; adaptation is faster than worst-case because it uses the estimated curve instead of worst-case margins, and smoother than raw online learning because the curve dampens wild swings when a single outlier arrives.
demo.metric_eq: Coverage rate = fraction of timesteps where true value fell inside the band; Band width = average (upper bound - lower bound); Regret = cumulative band width across all timesteps
demo.closing: The key outcome: COP's bands should be half as wide as naive worst-case during stability, yet maintain 90-percent coverage even when the regime flips to chaos.
